Book 1 of Phase 04

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 04                                                             Create the TaskFlow NestJS API

Step 1 - Confirm the monorepo before scaffolding
Run scaffolding commands from the TaskFlow repository root. This matters because the existing pnpm workspace should
own dependency installation and the root Git repository should remain the only repository.
From: taskflow\
Get-Location
node -v
pnpm -v
git status

Expected context

The working directory is the TaskFlow root, Node uses the Phase 00/01 locked LTS line, pnpm works, and Git reports the
existing repository rather than a new empty repository.

Step 2 - Scaffold the NestJS application
Use a temporary Nest CLI invocation instead of requiring a permanently global CLI. The CLI is a project-generation tool; the
framework packages themselves will live inside apps/api.
From: taskflow\
pnpm dlx @nestjs/cli@12.0.3 new apps/api --package-manager pnpm --skip-git --no-observe

--skip-git prevents the generated application from creating a nested .git directory. --no-observe answers the current CLI
observability prompt explicitly, keeping the course setup deterministic. The package-manager flag keeps installation aligned
with the workspace.

Why use pnpm dlx?

pnpm dlx downloads and runs the CLI command without requiring a global Nest CLI installation. The generated project still
records its own framework dependencies in apps/api/package.json.

Expected structure after scaffolding
taskflow/
|-- apps/
|   |-- web/
|   `-- api/
|       |-- src/
|       |    |-- app.controller.ts
|       |    |-- app.module.ts
|       |    |-- app.service.ts
|       |    `-- main.ts
|       |-- package.json
|       |-- nest-cli.json
|       `-- tsconfig.json
|-- packages/
|-- package.json
|-- pnpm-lock.yaml
`-- pnpm-workspace.yaml

Step 3 - Prove the generated API works before changing its
HTTP platform
From: taskflow\
cd apps/api
pnpm run start:dev

The first run is deliberately boring. It establishes a checkpoint: Nest can compile and start before we introduce Fastify. If
Fastify setup later fails, we can compare the failure against this known-good state.

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 04                                                                      Create the TaskFlow NestJS API

Checkpoint A

The API starts successfully. Keep this result in mind; it is your baseline before replacing the default Express platform adapter.

Understand the generated files before deleting anything
File                                        Responsibility

src/main.ts                                 Process entry point and Nest application bootstrap.

src/app.module.ts                           Root module; tells Nest what belongs to the application graph.

src/app.controller.ts                       Initial HTTP route boundary generated by the CLI.

src/app.service.ts                          Initial injectable provider used by the controller.

nest-cli.json                               Nest CLI/compiler project configuration.

package.json                                API scripts and dependencies owned by apps/api.

The generated controller/service are useful teaching material. We will first understand their relationship, then replace the starter
route with a Health feature. Deleting unfamiliar code before understanding it removes a learning opportunity.

NestJS and Fastify solve different problems
Layer                              What it contributes

NestJS                             Modules, dependency injection, controllers, providers, guards, pipes, interceptors and application
structure.

Fastify                            The concrete HTTP server/runtime that accepts requests and sends responses.

@nestjs/platform-fastify           The adapter that lets Nest run on Fastify while keeping Nest abstractions.

main.ts
application entry point

NestFactory.create(...)
starts Nest runtime

FastifyAdapter
selects HTTP platform

AppModule
root dependency graph

listen(4000)
opens local HTTP port

Figure - Bootstrap flow: main.ts chooses the platform, provides the root module, then starts listening.

Step 1 - Install the Nest Fastify platform adapter
From: taskflow\apps\api
pnpm add @nestjs/platform-fastify@12.0.3
pnpm remove @nestjs/platform-express

The course chooses Fastify intentionally, so keeping the Express platform package after the migration would create
ambiguity. Nest remains the application framework; only the concrete HTTP platform changes.

Fastify version policy

The course is locked to Fastify 5.x. The September 17, 2026 stable patch reference is 5.12.5. Fastify 6 is still an alpha line and is
not used in this course.

Step 2 - Change main.ts
apps/api/src/main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import {
FastifyAdapter,
NestFastifyApplication,
} from '@nestjs/platform-fastify';
import { AppModule } from './app.module.js';

async function bootstrap() {

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 04                                                                     Bootstrap and the Fastify Adapter

const app = await NestFactory.create<NestFastifyApplication>(
AppModule,
new FastifyAdapter(),
);

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 4000);
await app.listen(port, '127.0.0.1');
}

void bootstrap();

Read the file as an architectural sentence
●       NestFactory.create starts the Nest runtime.
●       AppModule is the root of the dependency graph.
●       FastifyAdapter selects Fastify as the HTTP platform implementation.
●       NestFastifyApplication gives TypeScript the correct application type for this platform.
●       listen opens the local port only after Nest has created and wired the application graph.

Why port 4000?

The frontend already uses the common Next.js development port 3000. The backend uses 4000 so both applications can run
simultaneously without fighting for the same port.

Step 3 - Verify the Fastify-backed API
From: taskflow\apps\api
pnpm run start:dev

Open the generated root route or use Invoke-WebRequest. The exact starter response matters less than the architectural
checkpoint: Nest is now running on Fastify and listening at localhost:4000.
In a second PowerShell window
(Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'http://127.0.0.1:4000/' -UseBasicParsing).Content

Checkpoint B

NestJS boots successfully using Fastify, and an HTTP request reaches the generated controller.

Fastify-specific caution
Once Fastify is the platform, recipes that depend directly on Express request/response objects or Express-only middleware
may not apply. Prefer Nest abstractions first; when platform-specific behavior is necessary, use the Fastify equivalent
deliberately.

The three core responsibilities
Concept                        Responsibility                                Question it answers

Module                         Composition / boundary                        Which related controllers and providers belong
together?

Controller                     HTTP boundary                                 Which request path and method should call which
handler?

Provider / Service             Reusable application behavior                 What work should happen after the HTTP boundary
delegates?

AppModule

root composition

HealthModule                                              Future TodoModule

health feature boundary                                            not built yet

HealthController                        HealthService

HTTP boundary                         application provider

Figure - Nest module graph: the root module composes feature modules; each feature groups closely related controllers and providers.

Read AppModule first
apps/api/src/app.module.ts - starter concept
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppController } from './app.controller.js';
import { AppService } from './app.service.js';

@Module({
imports: [],
controllers: [AppController],
providers: [AppService],
})
export class AppModule {}

The decorator is not decoration in the visual sense. It carries metadata that Nest reads while building the application graph.
The controller and service do not become available merely because their files exist; the module registers them into the graph.

Controller responsibility
Conceptual starter controller
@Controller()
export class AppController {
constructor(private readonly appService: AppService) {}

@Get()
getHello() {
return this.appService.getHello();
}
}

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 04                                                                    Modules, Controllers and Providers

The controller knows HTTP: route mapping and request handling. It delegates the actual response-producing behavior to a
provider. This distinction becomes more valuable once business rules are non-trivial.

Provider responsibility
Conceptual starter provider
@Injectable()
export class AppService {
getHello() {
return 'Hello World!';
}
}

A provider is a class managed by the Nest dependency injection container. Services are common providers, but providers can
also represent repositories, factories, clients or other reusable dependencies later in the course.

Why feature modules matter
A large backend should not place every controller and provider in AppModule. Feature modules group a cohesive capability
such as Health, Todos, Users or Projects. AppModule then becomes composition rather than a dumping ground.

Module boundary rule

Create a module when a group of controllers/providers belongs to one capability and should be composed as a unit. Do not
create one module per file, and do not create speculative Core/Common modules before a concrete responsibility exists.

Build HealthModule
From: taskflow\apps\api
pnpm exec nest generate module health
pnpm exec nest generate controller health --no-spec
pnpm exec nest generate service health --no-spec

The generators are not magic either. They create files and update module metadata. Always review the diff so you understand
what changed.
From: taskflow\
git diff -- apps/api

Checkpoint C

You can identify the root module, a feature module, an HTTP controller and an injectable service, and you can explain why they
are separate responsibilities.

Book 4 of Phase 04

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 04                                                        Dependency Injection and the Application Graph

Dependency injection is object wiring
The phrase dependency injection can sound abstract, but the practical question is simple: when HealthController needs
HealthService, who creates the service instance and gives it to the controller? In Nest, the IoC container performs that wiring
based on the providers registered in modules.

HealthController                                                                HealthService

declares dependency                                                           @Injectable provider

constructor type metadata

Nest IoC Container

creates + wires
instances

Figure - Dependency injection: the controller asks for a service; Nest resolves and supplies the registered provider.

Constructor injection
health.controller.ts - the consumer
@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
constructor(private readonly healthService: HealthService) {}
}

health.service.ts - the provider
@Injectable()
export class HealthService {
getStatus() {
return { status: 'ok' };
}
}

health.module.ts - the registration
@Module({
controllers: [HealthController],
providers: [HealthService],
})
export class HealthModule {}

These three snippets form one relationship: consumer, dependency, registration. If any side is missing, Nest cannot complete
the graph.

What Nest resolves at startup
1       Read AppModule and all imported modules.
2       Collect controller/provider metadata.
3       Create provider instances according to their registration and scope.
4       Inspect constructor dependencies and resolve each required provider.
5       Instantiate controllers with their dependencies already supplied.
6       Fail startup if the graph cannot be resolved.

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 04                                                          Dependency Injection and the Application Graph

Important default

Providers are generally singleton-scoped by default for the application lifecycle. Request scope exists, but using it everywhere
would increase complexity and overhead. This phase stays with the default scope.

Classic failure: Nest cannot resolve dependencies
Representative startup error
Nest can't resolve dependencies of the HealthController (?). Please make sure that the argument HealthService ... is av

Do not reinstall Nest. Read the dependency graph. Is HealthService decorated with @Injectable()? Is it listed in providers? Is
it exported/imported if consumed across module boundaries? Is the constructor asking for a runtime-resolvable class/token?

Interfaces are erased at runtime
TypeScript interfaces do not exist after compilation. Nest cannot inject an interface by type alone. Later, when we need
abstraction tokens, we will use explicit injection tokens. Do not introduce tokens early merely to imitate enterprise
architecture.

ASP.NET Core                        NestJS                                   Course interpretation

Program.cs / host bootstrap         main.ts + NestFactory                    Application startup and server bootstrap

Controller                          Controller                               HTTP endpoint boundary

Service registered in DI            Provider / @Injectable()                 Reusable application dependency

IServiceCollection / DI             Nest IoC container                       Creates and wires dependencies
container

Feature area / registration         Module                                   Groups and exposes related capabilities

Attribute routing                   Decorators such as @Controller and       Maps HTTP requests to handlers
@Get

Kestrel / host server               Fastify through platform adapter         Underlying HTTP server implementation

ASP.NET transfer

If you know ASP.NET Core DI, the mental model transfers well: constructor injection remains constructor injection. Nest
modules supply composition metadata where ASP.NET commonly uses IServiceCollection registration during startup.

import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HealthService } from './health.service.js';

@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
constructor(private readonly healthService: HealthService) {}

@Get()
getHealth() {
return this.healthService.getStatus();
}
}

@Controller('health') establishes the route prefix. @Get() registers an HTTP GET handler at that prefix. The method name
is for your code; the decorators determine the HTTP route.

@Post()                         POST /todos                                 Create - introduced later.

@Delete(':id')                  DELETE /todos/:id                           Delete - introduced later.

Return values become HTTP responses
Controller/service return value
return {
status: 'ok',
service: 'taskflow-api',

●    No validation pipe.

packages. Ask which layer produced the observable failure.

relationship

@Controller path

Port already in use
PowerShell
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 4000 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-Process -Id <PID>

The goal is to identify the process before terminating anything. Killing random Node processes can destroy unrelated
development sessions.

Missing provider registration
When Nest reports that it cannot resolve a constructor dependency, translate the message into a graph question: where is this
provider declared, and is it visible from the consumer's module?
Representative cause
@Module({
controllers: [HealthController],
// providers: [HealthService] <-- accidentally missing
})
export class HealthModule {}

Route returns 404
1      Confirm the process listening on port 4000 is the TaskFlow API.
2      Confirm AppModule imports HealthModule.
3      Confirm HealthModule registers HealthController.
4      Confirm @Controller('health') and @Get() produce the path you are requesting.
5      Restart only if watch mode did not pick up the structural change.

Wrong Fastify/Express assumption
If a tutorial tells you to manipulate an Express Response object or install Express-only middleware, stop and identify whether
that recipe is platform-specific. The TaskFlow backend uses Fastify through Nest. Prefer framework-agnostic Nest patterns
whenever possible.

Smallest-correction rule

Diagnose the layer, verify the hypothesis, make the smallest correction, then repeat the exact failing action. Recreating apps or
replacing configuration wholesale destroys evidence and teaches very little.

pnpm run build

Guided Build Lab — Phase 04: NestJS + Fastify Fundamentals

Purpose
Build a NestJS 12 API on Fastify and understand modules, controllers, providers, dependency injection, configuration, and request lifecycle.

Before you touch the code

Debugging Workshop — Phase 04: NestJS + Fastify Fundamentals

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
HTTP request -> Fastify adapter -> Nest middleware/guards/pipes -> Controller -> Service/provider -> Response

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Provider not registered/exported/imported correctly
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Adapter-specific plugins assumed to work like Express middleware
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Huge AppModule containing unrelated features
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — Business logic embedded in decorators/controllers
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — NestJS + Fastify Fundamentals

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 04 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Build a NestJS 12 API on Fastify and understand modules, controllers, providers, dependency injection, configuration, and request lifecycle.

Required artifact
A modular API with health endpoint and a small feature module whose controller and service responsibilities are separate.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can explain provider resolution.
• Can create a feature module from scratch.
• Can distinguish adapter and framework responsibilities.
• Can debug a dependency injection error.

Independent build sequence
1. Generate the API workspace and replace the default HTTP adapter with Fastify deliberately.
2. Create a HealthModule with controller and service instead of putting everything in AppController.
3. Inject the service through the constructor and explain how Nest resolves it.
4. Add configuration through Nest Config rather than reading process.env everywhere.
5. Trace one request with logs through bootstrap, controller, and service.
6. Break provider registration intentionally, read the dependency-resolution error, and repair the module graph.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

Evidence packet
